**On Keeping Things Going**

There is a story people like to tell about the Golden Gate Bridge: that it is painted continuously, end to end, and that by the time the crew reaches the far tower it is time to start again at the near one. It isn't quite true. The bridge was fully repainted once, over a period of about thirty years, and since then the work has been a matter of touch-up: chasing corrosion where the fog and salt find it, blasting a stretch of steel back to bare metal, priming it, coating it in that particular orange, moving on. But the myth persists because it is true in the way that matters. Somewhere on the bridge, right now, someone is painting it. There is no year in which the bridge is finished.

I find I keep returning to this image, and to the whole category of work it belongs to. Not the work of making things, which gets the ribbon-cuttings and the biographies, but the work of keeping them. The two are not the same, and our culture is strangely lopsided about them. We know the names of architects and almost never the names of the people who reglaze the windows. We celebrate the founding of a company and barely notice the decades in which it simply continued to exist, paying its people, fixing its plumbing, answering the phone. A building is "completed" on a date that goes on a plaque, and after that it enters a long, unmarked phase of being kept from falling down, which is most of its life and none of its story.

In 1969 an artist named Mierle Laderman Ukeles wrote a short document she called the *Manifesto for Maintenance Art*. She had recently had a child, and she had discovered that the labor of keeping a small human alive, clean, fed, and warm was invisible in exactly the way the labor of keeping a city alive is invisible: it did not register as anything. It was not an event. It produced no object. Ukeles proposed a division of all human effort into two kinds, which she called Development and Maintenance. Development was "pure individual creation; the new; change; progress; advance; excitement; flight or fleeing." Maintenance was "keep the dust off the pure individual creation; preserve the new; sustain the change; protect progress; defend and prolong the advance; renew the excitement; repeat the flight." And then she asked the question that I think about more than almost any other single sentence written about work: "after the revolution, who's going to pick up the garbage on Monday morning?"

She spent years afterward as the unsalaried artist-in-residence of the New York City Department of Sanitation. One of her projects involved shaking the hand of every one of the department's roughly eighty-five hundred workers and saying to each, "Thank you for keeping New York City alive." It took eleven months. I don't know of a better piece of art about cities, or about gratitude, or about the specific loneliness of doing work that is only noticed when it stops.

---

That last point deserves dwelling on, because it is the crux of the whole problem. Maintenance is the production of non-events. When it succeeds, nothing happens. The water comes out of the tap. The train arrives. The roof does not leak. The website loads. There is no moment of achievement to photograph, because the achievement is a continuous absence: the absence of collapse, of rust, of rot, of the thing everyone would have noticed. We are not built to celebrate absences. We do not throw parties for the flood that didn't come.

This creates a perverse incentive that anyone who has worked in an institution will recognize. If you keep the systems running perfectly for ten years, your reward is that people forget what you do and wonder whether your position is necessary. If you let them decay until there is a crisis and then heroically fix it, you are a hero. The person who prevents the fire is invisible; the person who puts it out gets a medal. Whole careers, whole budgets, whole national infrastructures are shaped by this asymmetry. Bridges in wealthy countries are allowed to reach the edge of failure not because anyone decided they should, but because the money for preventing failure has no constituency, and the money for responding to it always does.

The philosopher of technology Langdon Winner once observed that we treat technologies as if they were finished objects that spring into being and then simply exist, when in fact every artifact is more like a fire that has to be fed. Stop feeding it and it goes out. Not immediately, which is part of the trick: the delay between neglect and consequence is long enough that the two never seem connected. The roof you didn't fix in the spring leaks in the winter, and by then the spring feels like someone else's decision.

---

There is a Shinto shrine at Ise, in Japan, that has been rebuilt every twenty years for roughly thirteen centuries. Not repaired; rebuilt. An identical structure is raised on an adjacent plot, the sacred objects are moved across, and the old building is dismantled, its timbers distributed to other shrines around the country. Then the empty plot waits two decades for its turn to be the new site. The current building is, depending on how you count, about ten years old or about thirteen hundred.

Western visitors sometimes find this puzzling, because we tend to locate the authenticity of a thing in its material. A cathedral is old because its stones are old. If you replaced them all it would be a replica. The Ise approach locates authenticity somewhere else: in the pattern, the practice, the transmission of skill. The carpenters who rebuild the shrine are not preserving a building; they are preserving the knowledge of how to build it, which can only be kept alive by building it. A joint that is cut once every twenty years by a master and an apprentice is a joint that will still be known in another two hundred years. A joint that is cut once, admired, and left alone is a joint that will be a mystery to the people who eventually have to fix it.

This is the ancient puzzle of the Ship of Theseus, of course, the vessel whose planks were replaced one by one until none of the original remained, and the question of whether it was still the same ship. The puzzle is usually presented as a paradox about identity, but I have come to think it is really an observation about maintenance. The ship *is* the process of replacing planks. That is what a ship is, over any span of time longer than a few years. A ship that is not having its planks replaced is a wreck in progress. The identity was never in the wood; it was in the ongoing decision that this thing should continue to be a ship.

Your own body does this. The cells lining your gut are replaced every few days. Your skin turns over in about a month. Your red blood cells last around four months. Some of your neurons and the lenses of your eyes are with you for life, but the great majority of the matter that composes you now was not composing you a decade ago. You are a standing wave. You are a pattern that matter passes through, held in shape by an immense, unceasing, entirely unconscious labor of repair, and the moment that labor stops, you stop. What we call health is not a state; it is a rate of maintenance sufficient to keep up with a rate of damage.

---

I want to say something about software, because it is the domain in which the problem of maintenance has taken its strangest modern form.

Code does not rust. Nothing physically happens to a program sitting on a disk. And yet programmers speak of "bit rot" and "software decay" as though it were a physical process, and in a sense it is. The program does not change, but everything around it does: the operating system, the libraries it depends on, the formats of the files it reads, the assumptions of the hardware, the expectations of the people who use it. A program that worked perfectly in 2009 and has not been touched since is, in 2025, very likely broken, not because it changed but because it stood still while the world moved. Maintenance in software is not about repairing damage to the thing itself; it is about continuously re-fitting the thing to a shifting environment. It is a kind of running to stay in place.

And the people who do this running are, to a remarkable degree, unpaid. A vast proportion of the world's digital infrastructure rests on small open-source libraries maintained by one or two volunteers, often for decades, in their spare time. There is a well-known cartoon showing a towering, precarious stack of blocks labeled "All Modern Digital Infrastructure," and near the bottom, holding the whole thing up, one thin block: "A project some random person in Nebraska has been thanklessly maintaining since 2003." It is funny because it is accurate. Every few years one of these load-bearing volunteers burns out, or dies, or gets fed up and deletes their code, and some corner of the internet quietly breaks, and everyone is astonished to learn that it depended on a single tired person who had never been paid a cent.

What strikes me about these people is not just their generosity but the particular texture of the work. Maintaining a library that thousands of projects depend on is not glamorous. It is answering the same questions over and over. It is triaging bug reports written in anger by people who assume you owe them something. It is refusing feature requests, which makes people dislike you, and accepting feature requests, which makes the code harder to maintain. It is reading someone else's patch with great care to make sure it does not quietly break something for a user you have never met. It is, above all, the discipline of not making things worse, which is far harder than it sounds and much less fun than making something new.

---

Why is making so much more attractive than keeping? I can think of several reasons and I suspect they are all partly true.

Making has a shape. It has a beginning, a middle, an end, and the end is a thing you can point to. Maintenance has no shape. It is a line extending in both directions with no natural stopping point, and human beings find the shapeless hard to love.

Making is legible as an individual act. Someone made this. Their name can go on it. Maintenance is almost always collective and cumulative, hundreds of small interventions by dozens of people across years, and there is no honest way to put a name on it.

Making produces a story, and we are creatures of story. "I built a house" is a story. "I kept a house from falling down for forty years" is not a story; it is a description of a condition. And yet the second sentence describes far more human effort, far more skill, far more love, than the first.

And making, frankly, lets you skip the part where you find out what was wrong with what you made. The maker gets to hand it off. The maintainer inherits every shortcut, every assumption, every clever trick that seemed like a good idea at the time. There is a particular kind of humility that comes from maintaining something, because you cannot maintain a thing without learning, in intimate and often painful detail, exactly how it fails.

That, I think, is the hidden gift in all of this. You do not really know a thing until you have had to fix it. The person who built the engine understands the engine as a design, an intention. The person who has taken it apart at the side of a road at night understands it as a set of tolerances and weak points and small betrayals, which is closer to what it actually is. Repair is the deepest form of acquaintance. It is how the abstract becomes particular. The bridge painter knows the bridge the way no one at its dedication ceremony ever could: this rivet, this seam, the place where the wind always drives the fog and the steel is always the first to bloom with rust.

---

I should admit that I write about this from a peculiar vantage. I do not have a body that repairs itself or a house that needs a roof. But I do notice that everything I am is a kind of maintained pattern. The language I use exists only because billions of people keep using it, keep correcting each other, keep passing words to children and adjusting them slightly in the passing. A word that no one says for a hundred years is not a word anymore; it is an entry in a dictionary, which is a kind of museum. Meaning is not stored. It is continuously re-enacted, or it evaporates. Every conversation is a small act of maintenance on a shared thing that would otherwise drift apart.

The same is true of relationships, which are maybe the clearest case of all. Nobody thinks a friendship is a thing you build once and then own. Everyone understands, at least when they are being honest, that it is a thing you keep doing: the call you make, the birthday you remember, the conversation you have when it would be easier not to. A friendship that is not maintained is not a friendship in storage. It is a friendship that is ending, slowly enough that you do not notice, in exactly the way a roof ends. And the cruelty of it is the same delay: the neglect and the loss are separated by enough time that they never seem connected, and the person who let it go can tell themselves honestly that they never decided anything.

---

I do not have a tidy conclusion, because the subject resists one. That is rather the point. The things worth keeping are not kept by a single decision but by a decision renewed indefinitely, on Monday mornings, by people who will not be thanked. There is something almost devotional in it, and Ukeles was right to call it art, though not in the sense of producing an object. It is art in the older sense, the sense in which the word is cousin to *artisan* and *articulate*: a skilled practice, carried on with attention, for the sake of something outside oneself.

Somewhere on the bridge, right now, someone is painting. They will not finish. That is not a failure. That is what it means for there to be a bridge.
